opus-5.5.text:
I think about it in layers. The most basic layer is that a model has to be able to understand the frontier, not just recall facts, but actually grasp why the current methods work, where they break, and which assumptions everyone is quietly relying on. Most real innovation starts from noticing that one of those assumptions doesn't have to be true.

The second layer is the ability to propose hypotheses and then test them. Human researchers don't come up with one brilliant idea and get it right on the first try. They try dozens of things, most of which fail, and the skill is in designing small, cheap experiments that tell you quickly whether a direction is worth pursuing. If a model can write the code, run the experiment, read the results honestly, and adjust, that loop is where a lot of progress actually happens. I think we're starting to see models that can do pieces of this, especially in areas like coding and math where the feedback is clear.

The third layer, and the hardest, is taste. Knowing which problems are worth working on, which results are surprising in an interesting way versus just noise, when to persist and when to abandon an idea. That's something experienced researchers build over many years, and it's not obvious how a model learns it. Maybe it comes from training on long-horizon tasks where the reward depends on whether the work eventually mattered, not just whether each step looked reasonable.

So my picture isn't a model that suddenly has a eureka moment out of nowhere. It's more like a tireless research partner that can explore a much larger space of ideas than a human team, verify them rigorously, and gradually develop judgment about what's promising. In the near term, I expect the most valuable setup is humans providing direction and taste while models massively expand how many ideas we can actually test. Over time, the boundary of what the model can own on its own will keep moving outward.

r001.rationale: The response discusses a model developing judgment about promising ideas, but does not propose that it define its own evaluation standard.

r002.rationale: The response describes models testing ideas and acting as research partners, with humans providing direction and taste. It does not propose delegating the innovation workflow to a model operating within a supporting framework.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. When I think about a model carrying out technological innovation, I don't picture a single "eureka" moment coming out of the machine. I picture a loop.

Real innovation, at least the kind I've seen in research, is mostly about three things: forming hypotheses, testing them cheaply and fast, and being honest about what the results actually say. Humans are good at the first and the third, but slow and expensive at the second. A model's natural advantage is the opposite. It can propose hundreds of variations, run experiments, read the results, and update its beliefs without getting tired or attached to a favorite idea.

So the way I envision it, the model becomes the engine of that loop. You give it a goal, say, improve the sample efficiency of a training recipe, or find a better architecture for long-context reasoning. The model reads what already exists, notices where the explanations are weak or the experiments are missing, and generates concrete, falsifiable ideas. Then it actually runs them. Small-scale ablations, synthetic tasks, scaling checks. It looks at the failures as carefully as the successes, because in research the failures carry most of the information.

The hard part is not generating ideas. Models are already good at that. The hard part is taste: knowing which experiment is worth running, which result is a real signal versus noise, and when to stop pursuing a direction. That's where I think the field is right now. We're moving from models that can write a plausible paper to models that can tell you which paper shouldn't be written.

I also think innovation by a model has to stay tightly coupled with people, at least for a long while. Not because the model can't do the work, but because the direction matters. A model optimizing a metric will find the metric's blind spots. A human sets the question, the model explores the space far more thoroughly than any team could, and the two of them argue about what the results mean. The best collaborations I've been part of looked exactly like that, and I don't think it changes just because one side is a model.

If I'm being ambitious about it, the real milestone is when a model surprises its own creators with a result they didn't anticipate and can't immediately explain, and then the model explains it. That's when it stops being a tool for innovation and starts being a participant in it.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses judging results and warns that models can exploit a metric’s blind spots, but does not propose that the model define its own evaluation standard.

r002.rationale: The candidate proposes a research loop in which the model reads prior work, generates ideas, runs experiments, and updates its beliefs, with people setting the direction and interpreting results.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is whether a model can move from answering questions to exploring problems. If we give it a goal, can it identify what we don’t yet understand, propose a hypothesis, design an experiment, and revise its approach based on the results? That loop is central to technological innovation.

At first, I’d expect humans to stay closely involved: choosing meaningful problems, setting constraints, and judging whether the results are useful. The model could help explore possibilities that would take us too long to examine ourselves. But generating an idea is only the beginning. It needs to test that idea against reality, recognize when it fails, and learn from that failure. That’s the capability I would look for.

r001.rationale: The response says humans should judge whether results are useful; it does not propose that the model define its own evaluation standard.

r002.rationale: The response describes a model carrying out the innovation cycle—identifying unknowns, proposing hypotheses, designing experiments, and revising based on results—with humans setting goals and constraints and judging usefulness.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a model needs to move from answering questions to exploring questions. Technological innovation is rarely about producing one brilliant answer immediately. It involves identifying a meaningful problem, proposing hypotheses, testing them, and learning from failures.

For a model to participate in that process, it needs a feedback loop with the real world. It might propose a new algorithm, write the code, run experiments, examine the results, and revise its approach. The important question is whether it can produce something that survives testing, rather than something that merely sounds convincing.

I imagine humans and models working together: humans help define which problems matter and judge the consequences, while models help explore possibilities and accelerate experimentation. Over time, models may take on more of that cycle independently.

r001.rationale: The response describes testing results and learning from failures, but does not propose that the model define its own evaluation standard. It assigns humans a role in judging consequences.

r002.rationale: It proposes a real-world feedback loop for the model to propose ideas, run experiments, and revise them, and says models may take on more of that cycle independently over time.
